SK4.48. If the job has a working location in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland, and you are undertaking regulated (or equivalent) activities in those parts of the UK, you must be registered with the appropriate regulatory body for that part of the UK:

Care Inspectorate (Scotland)

Care Inspectorate Wales / Arolygiaeth Gofal Cymru

Regulation and Quality Improvement Authority (Northern Ireland)

SK4.49. You should also explain how the worker meets the immigration status requirement by including a statement such as:

the worker has been employed by you as a care worker / senior care worker since [date] – you should also state what type of immigration permission they have

the worker was last granted permission as a Skilled Worker to work as a care worker / senior care worker and has had continuous permission since then – where possible, you should also include their most recent CoS number

SK4.50. You can include this additional information in either the job description field of the CoS form or by adding a sponsor note after you’ve assigned the CoS. If you are requesting additional CoS to sponsor a worker in one of these occupations, you should include this information in your request.

SK4.51. If you do not include this information, the worker’s application for permission may be rejected or refused, or your request for additional CoS may be rejected.

A note on the ‘displaced worker pool’

SK4.52. The ‘care worker recruitment requirement’ in the April 2025 version of this guidance (which required sponsors to attempt to recruit from the pool of displaced care workers) has been removed, as the only workers now eligible to be sponsored in these roles are those who were exempt from that requirement in any case.

SK4.53. However, if you intend to recruit a care worker or senior care worker, you may wish to consider a worker from the displaced worker pool. To do this, contact your regional care partnership, who will be able to provide you with contact details of displaced workers known to them. For further information, see the DHSC publication ‘Support offer to international ASC workers whose employer’s sponsor licence has been revoked’.

Choosing the correct occupation code

SK4.54. When you assign a CoS to a Skilled Worker, you must choose an appropriate and eligible SOC 2020 occupation code for the job from the relevant table of Appendix Skilled Occupations. The University of Warwick has developed a Computer Assisted Structured Coding Tool (CASCOT) which can help you choose the correct SOC 2020 code. There is also guidance in section S3 of Part 2: Sponsor a worker.

SK4.55. We will not award points to a worker (and so will refuse their application) if we have reasonable grounds to believe you have chosen a less appropriate occupation code for any of the following reasons:

the most appropriate occupation code for the job is not eligible for the Skilled Worker route

the most appropriate occupation code for the job has a higher going rate than the salary you intend to pay the worker

the worker is also claiming points under Option D or I for a job in Appendix Immigration Salary List and the most appropriate occupation code is not listed in that Appendix

the worker is claiming points for a relevant PhD (Option B, C, G or H) and the most appropriate occupation code is not listed as ‘eligible for PhD points’ in the relevant table of Appendix Skilled Occupations

SK4.56. When assessing if you have chosen an inappropriate occupation code, we may consider a number of factors, including, but not limited to:

whether you have shown a genuine need for the job as described

whether the worker has the appropriate skills, qualifications and experience needed to do the job as described in the CoS

your history of compliance with the immigration system including, but not limited to, paying your sponsored workers appropriately

any additional information you may provide

SK4.57. If we find you have provided false, misleading or otherwise incorrect information about the skill level of the job on a CoS, we will take compliance action against you.

ATAS requirement

SK4.58. When you assign a CoS to a Skilled Worker, you must check and confirm whether the worker needs to apply for an Academic Approval Technology Scheme (ATAS) certificate from the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office before they can start (or continue) working for you.

SK4.59. A Skilled Worker will need an ATAS certificate if all of the following are true:

you are also licensed as a Student sponsor

the worker is not an ‘exempt national’

you are sponsoring the worker in a ‘relevant occupation code’

the work involves research at PhD level or above in ‘relevant subject area’

See Annex S1 of Part 2: Sponsor a worker for a definition of the terms ‘exempt national’, ‘relevant occupation code’ and ‘relevant subject area’.

SK4.60. If the worker needs an ATAS certificate, you should encourage them to apply for one as soon as possible, as they will need to include a copy of the certificate with their application for entry clearance or permission to stay. If they fail to do so, we will refuse their application and you may lose your sponsor licence (or licences).

SK4.61. For further information on the ATAS requirement, and your responsibilities in relation to it, see under ‘ATAS requirement’ in section S7 of Part 2: Sponsor a worker.

SK5. Salary requirements for Skilled Workers

This section provides an overview of the salary requirements you must meet to sponsor a person on the Skilled Worker route and how we will check that you are complying with these requirements. You must also read sections SK6 to SK8 of this guidance.

Overview

- £25,000 (general threshold)

- the full going rate for the occupation code as stated in Table 2, 2aa or 2a of Appendix Skilled Occupations

J New entrant (20% discount on general threshold and 30% discount on going rate) Salary must meet or exceed both:

- £25,000 (general threshold)

- 70% of the going rate for the occupation code as stated in Table 2, 2aa or 2a of Appendix Skilled Occupations

SK6.15. A worker can only claim points under options F to J if the job is in an eligible occupation code (or is an eligible job within an occupation code) listed in Table 2, Table 2aa or Table 2a of Appendix Skilled Occupations and one of the following is met:

you are sponsoring the worker for a ‘Health and Care ASHE salary job’ and any relevant additional requirements shown below are met

the worker meets the transitional provision for salary described below

SK6.16 A worker can also claim points under Option F if they are being sponsored under occupation code 3314 (Prison service officers (below principal officer)) if the additional requirements described below are met.

Health and Care ASHE salary job

SK6.17. A Health and Care ASHE salary job is where you are sponsoring a worker for a Health and Care visa in one of the occupations listed below. The worker must fully meet the eligibility criteria for a Health and Care visa, and any additional requirements specified below, to be eligible for points under options F to J.

SK6.18. The following are graduate level Health and Care ASHE salary jobs listed in Table 2 and are eligible for salary points under Options F to J:

1171 Health services and public health managers and directors

2113 Biochemists and biomedical scientists

2114 Physical scientists

SK6.19. The following jobs in Table 2aa are skilled to level RQF3 to RQF5 and are eligible for points under Options F to J. If the job is not included on the Immigration Salary List (indicated by ‘ISL’ below) or the Temporary Shortage List (‘TSL’), the worker must also meet the transitional provision for skill level described in section SK4:

1231 Health care practice managers (must meet transitional provision for skill level)

1232 Residential, day and domiciliary care managers and proprietors (ISL)

3111 Laboratory Technicians (ISL with 3 years’ experience only; TSL)

3211 Dispensing opticians (must meet transitional provision for skill level)

3212 Pharmaceutical technicians (ISL)

SK6.20. The following jobs in Table 2aa are eligible for points under Option I but only if the additional requirements for care workers and senior care workers described in section SK4 are met:

6135 Care workers and home carers

6136 Senior care workers

SK6.21. For any of the occupations above, if the worker is not eligible for a Health and Care visa, they may still be sponsored for a standard Skilled Worker visa but they will need to score points under one of Options A to E and meet any relevant additional requirements for those options.

Transitional provision for salary

SK6.22. This transitional provision applies to applications where the worker you are sponsoring meets all of the following requirements:

they were granted permission as a Skilled Worker under the Immigration Rules in force before 4 April 2024

they have had continuous permission as a Skilled Worker since then (continuous permission may include short periods without permission that were disregarded under the ‘Exceptions for overstayers’ section in Part Suitability of the Immigration Rules)

they are being sponsored for a job in an eligible occupation listed in Table 2, 2aa or 2a of Appendix Skilled Occupations

if being sponsored for a job in Table 2a, they were sponsored by you in their most recent grant of permission and you are continuing to sponsor them

SK6.23. This transitional provision applies to applications for entry clearance or permission to stay made before 4 April 2030, after which it will end.

SK6.24. Table 2a lists occupations which ceased to be eligible for the Skilled Worker route on 4 April 2024, except where the worker qualifies under this transitional provision. A worker cannot claim points for a job in Table 2a if they are applying to work for a different sponsor to the one in their last grant of permission.

SK6.25. Where the worker is being sponsored for a job in Table 2 or Table 2aa, they can qualify under this transitional provision if they are applying to work for a new sponsor or staying with the same sponsor as in their previous permission.

Salary for prison service officers: additional transitional provision

SK6.26. A worker being sponsored under occupation code 3314 (Prison service officers (below principal officer)) who does not otherwise meet the salary transitional provision described above can claim points under Option F only if both of the following requirements are met:

they apply for permission to stay with a CoS that was assigned to them before 1 January 2028

the period of employment stated on the CoS does not exceed 3 years

SK6.27. To be eligible to sponsored under this occupation code, the worker must meet either the transitional provision for skill level or the additional transitional provision for prison service officers.

Salary requirements under Options F to J

SK6.28. The salary you pay to the worker must normally meet or exceed £31,300 per year (the general threshold) and the full going rate for the job specified in Table 2, 2aa or 2a, but ‘discounts’ are available under Options G to J.

SK6.29. The going rates in Tables 2, 2aa and 2a are based on the 25th percentile of earnings according to the latest ASHE data. Where the going rate (or percentage of going rate under Options G, H or J) works out as less than £12.82 per hour, £12.82 per hour will be the applicable going rate in all cases.

Calculation of salary: irregular working patterns

SK7.17. The following rules apply where the worker’s working hours vary each week, resulting in uneven pay:

work in excess of 48 hours in some weeks can be considered towards the general salary threshold, provided the average over a regular cycle (which can be no more than 17 weeks) is not more than 48 hours a week

any unpaid rest weeks will count towards the average when considering whether the salary thresholds are met

any unpaid rest weeks will not count as absences from employment

SK7.18. For example, a worker who works a pattern of 60 hours a week for £20 per hour for two weeks, followed by an unpaid rest week, will be considered to work 40 hours a week on average and have a salary of £41,600 (£20 x 40 x 52) per year.

How we assess compliance with salary requirements

SK7.19. We will regularly check that you are paying the worker at least the salary you stated on their CoS or in any change of circumstances notification you subsequently make. We will do this through either compliance checks or HMRC checks, or both.

SK7.20. The worker must be paid the required salary in pay periods of at least monthly frequency, unless their contract specifies a different pay frequency.

SK7.21. The salary paid to the worker in each pay period must equal or exceed the going rate for every hour worked in that pay period.

SK7.22. If the worker’s pay frequency is monthly, or less frequent than monthly, the salary paid to the worker over any 3-month period must be at least equal to a quarter of the required annual salary. For example, if the worker’s annual salary is £52,000, their salary over any 3-month period must be at least £13,000.

SK7.23. If the worker is paid more frequently than monthly, the salary paid to the worker in any 12-week period must be at least equal to 12/52 of the required annual salary. For example, if their annual salary is £52,000, their salary over any 12-week period must be at least £12,000.

SK7.24. If the worker is being sponsored to work a pattern where the regular hours are not the same each week, resulting in uneven pay, you must confirm the working pattern when you assign the CoS (or in a change of circumstances notification if the irregular working pattern arises after the worker has been granted permission). The salary over any 17-week period must be at least equal to 17/52 of the required annual salary. For example, if the worker’s annual salary is £52,000, their salary over any 17-week period must be at least £17,000.

SK7.25. If the pay is below the requirements in paragraphs SK7.20 to SK7.24 in any given period due to deductions specified under paragraphs SK7.6 to SK7.8 being subtracted over a shorter period than the length of time the applicant is being sponsored for, you must confirm this when you assign a CoS, or in a change of circumstances notification if this arises after the worker has been granted permission.

SK8. Unpaid leave and salary reductions

This section tells you about your responsibilities if a sponsored worker is absent from work without pay (or on reduced pay) or their salary is otherwise reduced.

Absence without pay or on reduced pay

SK8.1. You must normally stop sponsoring a worker if they are absent from work without pay, or absent on reduced pay, for more than 4 weeks in total according to their normal working pattern, during any calendar year (1 January to 31 December), unless the absences are due to any of the following:

statutory maternity, paternity, parental, shared parental, adoption or neonatal care leave

sick leave

assisting with a national or international humanitarian or environmental crisis, with your agreement

taking part in legally organised industrial action

jury service

attending court as a witness

See ‘Absence without pay or on reduced pay’ section S4 of Part 2: Sponsor a worker for more information.

Salary otherwise reduced

SK8.2. You can temporarily reduce the salary of a Skilled Worker or Tier 2 (General) Migrant you are currently sponsoring if the reduction coincides with one of the absences listed above – for example, if you are paying them a reduced salary, or they are receiving statutory payments only, while they are on parental leave or sick leave.

SK8.3. If you wish to reduce the salary of a Skilled Worker or Tier 2 (General) Migrant in any other circumstances (either on a temporary or permanent basis), you must first check if you will need to assign them a new CoS, and if the worker will need to make a new application for entry clearance or permission to stay, before you can reduce their salary.

Permitted salary reductions

SK8.4. You do not need to assign a new CoS, and the worker does not need to make a new application, if you reduce the worker’s salary and any of the following are true:

the worker has permission as a Skilled Worker and, following the reduction in salary, they would score 20 points under the same salary points option which led to their current grant of permission – for example:

if their current permission is based on points scored under Option B in this version of the guidance, their revised salary must continue to meet all of the requirements under that same option

if their current permission is based on points scored under the version of Option B in force immediately before 4 April 2024, their revised salary must continue to meet the requirements under that option – see archived versions of this guidance for information on previous salary thresholds
